stem: What distinguishes working memory from long-term memory in an agent context?

options.text: Working memory requires a special password to access
Working memory is immediately available in the current context with no retrieval step, unlike long-term memory
Working memory is always larger than long-term memory
There is no actual difference between the two

explanation.why_correct: The defining distinction is that working memory is directly present in the current context and usable without any retrieval step, while long-term memory requires a deliberate retrieval step before it becomes usable.

why_incorrect.A: Access to memory is not gated by anything resembling a password; this is an irrelevant distractor.
why_incorrect.C: Long-term memory can typically store far more than working memory, which is bounded by the context window -- the opposite of this claim.
why_incorrect.D: There is a clear, meaningful, and well-documented difference between the two memory types.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Working memory needs no retrieval step; long-term memory does -- this is the core distinguishing trait.

stem: Why is simply storing information in long-term memory not sufficient on its own to benefit an agent's future behavior?

options.text: Long-term memory can only ever store exactly one fact at a time
Long-term memory storage is purely decorative and serves no function
Information in long-term memory automatically appears in every future conversation with no retrieval needed
Stored information must still be actively retrieved into working memory at the right moment to actually influence reasoning

explanation.why_correct: Information sitting in long-term storage provides no benefit until a retrieval mechanism actually brings it back into working memory at a relevant moment -- storage alone, without effective retrieval, doesn't influence behavior.

why_incorrect.B: Long-term memory storage does serve a real function -- it just requires effective retrieval to realize that function's benefit.
why_incorrect.C: Long-term memory does NOT automatically appear in every future conversation; it specifically requires an explicit retrieval step, which is exactly the point being made.
why_incorrect.A: Long-term memory can store many facts; there's no such severe one-fact-at-a-time limitation.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Long-term memory's value is realized only through effective retrieval -- storage without retrieval provides no actual behavioral benefit.

stem: A team designs an agent that relies exclusively on an ever-growing context window with no long-term memory system at all, intending to simply never truncate anything. What problem does this design eventually face?

options.text: Even a very large context window is still finite, so the design will eventually hit a limit as the conversation grows indefinitely
No problem at all, since context windows have no upper bound in practice
The agent will gain the ability to remember things across completely separate sessions automatically
This design is strictly superior to any system that uses long-term memory

explanation.why_correct: Any context window, however large, is still finite -- a design that assumes unlimited growth will eventually hit that limit as the conversation or task continues to grow indefinitely.

why_incorrect.B: All context windows have some finite upper bound in practice, even if large; assuming otherwise is the exact flaw being described.
why_incorrect.C: A large context window within a single session does not provide cross-session persistence; that specifically requires long-term memory, which this design lacks.
why_incorrect.D: This design has a real limitation (eventual context exhaustion and no cross-session persistence) that a combined working/long-term memory design would not have.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Even very large context windows are finite -- relying solely on an ever-growing window is not a scalable substitute for a proper long-term memory system.
